requirements.hypothesis: LiFlow is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: LiFlow trained on 25 ps ab initio molecular dynamics trajectories can generate stable trajectories up to 1 ns in larger (4 × 4 × 4) supercells, reproducing lithium self‑diffusivity, activation energies, and temperature dependence comparable to long AIMD simulations.
LiFlow predicts lithium mean‑squared displacement with a Spearman rank correlation of 0.7–0.8 on unseen material compositions, enabling screening of high‑diffusivity electrolytes.
LiFlow qualitatively captures ion transport behavior in sodium‑based conductors despite being trained only on lithium‑containing materials.

LiFlow achieves speed‑ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.
The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

A direct regression (Regressor) model yields higher mean‑squared‑displacement errors than the generative LiFlow model, demonstrating the necessity of generative modeling for accurate atomic transport simulation.

Reproducibility of DFT calculations

The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.
Electronic convergence stability
BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths.

Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.

requirements.hypothesis: The AFLOW Standard for High-Throughput Materials Science Calculations is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: The AFLOW standard enables reproducible high-throughput DFT calculations through standardized parameter sets for k-point density, energy cut-offs, exchange-correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, DFT+U parameters, and convergence criteria.
BANDS calculations use 128 k-points per segment for single element structures and 20 k-points for compounds along high-symmetry paths.

Electronic convergence criteria are δEelec = 10⁻⁵ eV and ionic convergence criteria are δEion = 10⁻⁴ eV for Elements database entries, while all other databases use δEelec = 10⁻³ eV and δEion = 10⁻² eV.

evidence_comparisons.text: Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) enables graph neural networks to handle variable output dimensions by incorporating virtual nodes that resemble phonon dynamical matrices.

requirements.hypothesis: DeepH-E3 is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.
DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.
DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.

requirements.hypothesis: D4FT is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: D4FT correctly predicts the paramagnetic ground state of O₂ and the diamagnetic ground state of CO₂ by comparing spin‑restricted and spin‑unrestricted calculations.
D4FT scales to carbon clusters up to C₁₈₀, achieving wall‑clock runtimes an order of magnitude faster (≈1100 s for C₁₈₀) than PySCF, GPAW, Psi4, and JAX‑SCF.
D4FT converges to a self‑consistent Kohn‑Sham solution that satisfies the eigenfunction condition.

The QR‑based reparameterization used in D4FT preserves the orthonormal constraints of Kohn‑Sham orbitals, making the search space equivalent to the original orthogonal function space, as proved in Proposition 3.1, and can be interpreted as projected gradient descent on the orthogonal constraint set.

evidence_comparisons.text: MLIP models trained on OMat24 achieve F1 scores above 0.9 for stability prediction and 20 meV/atom accuracy for formation energy on Matbench Discovery, with all five top-performing models on the Matbench Discovery leaderboard exclusively trained on OMat24.

The eSEN model achieves an F1 score of 0.925 and energy-above-hull MAE of 18 meV/atom when pretrained on OMat24, with eSEN and equiformerV2 models with DeNS outperforming their non-DeNS counterparts and all other third-party models in the Matbench Discovery benchmark task.

Accelerated discovery of stable inorganic crystals
Thermodynamic stability prediction from unrelaxed crystal structures

Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).

EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.

requirements.hypothesis: EquiformerV2 is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: EquiformerV2 achieves the highest success rate in the AdsorbML algorithm and enables a 2x reduction in DFT calculations needed for computing adsorption energies.
EquiformerV2 trained on only OC22 (8.4M structures) achieves better results than GemNet-OC trained on both OC20 (130M structures) and OC22, demonstrating significantly better data efficiency.

EquiformerV2 incorporates three architectural improvements: attention re-normalization, separable S2 activation, and separable layer normalization, replacing SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions to efficiently incorporate higher-degree tensors.

EquiformerV2 can scale Lmax to 6 or 8 on OC20 dataset using eSCN convolutions that reduce computational cost from O(L^6) to O(L^3), whereas original Equiformer is impractical for Lmax > 2 on large-scale datasets.

The eSEN model achieves an F1 score of 0.925 and energy-above-hull MAE of 18 meV/atom when pretrained on OMat24, with eSEN and equiformerV2 models with DeNS outperforming their non-DeNS counterparts and all other third-party models in the Matbench Discovery benchmark task.
OC20 S2EF-2M
OC20 IS2RE
EQUIFORMERV2: IMPROVED EQUIVARIANT TRANSFORMER FOR SCALING TO HIGHER-DEGREE REPRESENTATIONS

Extrapolation performance degrades with increasing WBM batch number for most models, especially Wrenformer and Voronoi RF, while universal interatomic potential models (e.g., EquiformerV2, ORB) show minimal degradation across batches.

OMat24 comprises over 118 million DFT calculations across diverse chemistries, materials, and configurations for inorganic bulk materials, making it up to 2 orders of magnitude larger than other openly available datasets in terms of number of single-point calculations.

requirements.hypothesis: Machine Learning-Guided Discovery of Temperature-Induced Solid-Solid Phase Transitions in Inorganic Materials is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.

Several predicted solid‑solid transitions show large entropy changes exceeding 300 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ (e.g., Li₃MnF₇: 342.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, PnCl₂: 338.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, Fe₄OF₇: 252.1 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹), while the highest entropy changes (> 400 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹) are limited to transitions above 450 K and occur exclusively in nonpolar‑nonpolar categories, reducing their relevance for room‑temperature applications.

evidence_comparisons.text: Benchmarking Materials Property Prediction Methods: The Matbench Test Set and Automatminer Reference Algorithm

Matbench v0.1 is a benchmark suite containing 13 supervised machine learning tasks (10 regression, 3 classification) for materials property prediction, with dataset sizes ranging from 312 to 132,752 samples.
Matbench experimental metallicity classification

Matbench contains data from 10 density functional theory-derived and experimental sources including Materials Project, Zhuo et al., Landolt-Bornstein Handbook, Castelli et al., JARVIS DFT 2D, and Citrine Informatics.
Matbench v0.1

Graph networks (CGCNN and MEGNet) far outperform traditional ML algorithms on formation energy prediction tasks, with MEGNet decisively outperforming Automatminer for the PhDOS task; among nine structure-based tasks, Automatminer and MEGNet each achieve best scores on 4 tasks.

By extracting per‑atom site energies in perovskites, the model reveals that large‑radius elements stabilize the A site and group 4‑6 elements stabilize the B site, and using these insights the high‑throughput search space for stable perovskites is reduced by a factor of seven (from 18,928 to 228 candidates).

evidence_comparisons.text: M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
M3GNet is an extension of MEGNet model to include 3-body interactions, explicit atomic coordinates, and 3×3 crystal lattice matrix.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

evidence_comparisons.text: The computational cost of LiFlow scales linearly with the number of atoms (O(n)), in contrast to the cubic scaling (O(n³)) of ab initio molecular dynamics.

LiFlow achieves speed‑ups of up to ~600,000× over ab initio molecular dynamics (and ~400× over MLIP), predicting a 1 ns trajectory in 48 s for a 2 × 2 × 1 LGPS supercell and 352 s for a 4 × 4 × 4 supercell.

requirements.hypothesis: GNoME is suitable for accelerating electronic structure calculations.

evidence_comparisons.text: GNoME enables efficient discovery of materials with 4+ unique elements, which have been difficult for previous discovery efforts.
Final GNoME models predict energies with a mean absolute error of 11 meV per atom on relaxed structures, improved from 21 meV per atom in the initial model trained on Materials Project data.

Large-scale pretraining of MLIPs on GNoME dataset enables models with unprecedented zero-shot accuracy on downstream AIMD data, outperforming state-of-the-art NequIP models trained on hundreds of structures from the target distribution.
GNoME-driven molecular dynamics simulations on 623 materials with previously unseen compositions enable classification of unseen compositions as superionic conductors in comparison with AIMD.

GNNs trained on large and diverse first-principles calculations increase the number of stable crystals by more than an order of magnitude, with scaling showing consistent power-law improvements in MLIP accuracy and generalization on out-of-distribution structural tasks.

Crystal structures, data, and software for analyzing stable crystals, phase diagrams, static GNN, and interatomic potentials will be made available at the Google DeepMind materials_discovery GitHub repository and via the Materials Project with permanent DOI link 10.17188/2009989.

evidence_comparisons.text: CHGNet enables nanosecond‑scale molecular dynamics simulations of garnet Li₃La₃Te₂O₁₂, yielding lithium self‑diffusion coefficients with quantified uncertainty.
CHGNet integrates magnetic moment labels as a proxy for atomic charge, enabling inference of atomic charges and accurate differentiation of oxidation states such as V³⁺/V⁴⁺ and Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺.

In charge‑informed molecular dynamics of Li₀.₅MnO₂ at 1100 K, CHGNet predicts the emergence of Mn²⁺ after ~0.8 ns, coinciding with a ~50 meV/oxygen reduction in potential energy and the formation of a spinel‑like phase, indicating a correlation between charge disproportionation and phase transformation.
